body {
  font-family: "GT Standard", sans-serif;
}

/* ===========================================
   Typography System (from Figma Design)
   =========================================== */

/* Heading Styles - Light Mode */
h1 {
  font-family: "GT Standard", sans-serif;
  font-weight: 500;
  font-size: 32px;
  line-height: 38px;
  letter-spacing: 0.01em;
  color: #000000;
}

h2 {
  font-family: "GT Standard", sans-serif;
  font-weight: 500;
  font-size: 28px;
  line-height: 32px;
  letter-spacing: -0.02em;
  color: #121516;
}

h3 {
  font-family: "GT Standard", sans-serif;
  font-weight: 500;
  font-size: 22px;
  line-height: 26px;
  letter-spacing: -0.02em;
  color: #121516;
}

h4 {
  font-family: "GT Standard", sans-serif;
  font-weight: 600;
  font-size: 18px;
  line-height: 21px;
  letter-spacing: -0.02em;
  color: #121516;
}

h5 {
  font-family: "GT Standard", sans-serif;
  font-weight: 500;
  font-size: 17px;
  line-height: 22px;
  letter-spacing: -0.02em;
  color: rgba(18, 21, 22, 0.9);
}

h6 {
  font-family: "GT Standard", sans-serif;
  font-weight: 500;
  font-size: 15px;
  line-height: 17px;
  letter-spacing: -0.02em;
  color: #121516;
}

/* Heading Styles - Dark Mode */
.dark h1 {
  color: #FFFFFF;
}

.dark h2 {
  color: #F7F7F8;
}

.dark h3 {
  color: #F7F7F8;
}

.dark h4 {
  color: #F7F7F8;
}

.dark h5 {
  color: rgba(247, 247, 248, 0.9);
}

.dark h6 {
  color: #F7F7F8;
}

/* Paragraph Styles - Light Mode */
p,
.prose [data-as="p"],
.prose span[data-as="p"] {
  font-family: "GT Standard", sans-serif;
  font-weight: 300;
  font-size: 16px;
  line-height: 140%;
  letter-spacing: -0.03em;
  color: #545658;
}

/* Paragraph Large */
.text-lg, .paragraph-large {
  font-weight: 300;
  font-size: 18px;
  line-height: 140%;
  letter-spacing: -0.03em;
  color: #545658;
}

/* Paragraph Bold */
strong, b, .font-medium {
  font-weight: 500;
}

/* Paragraph Small */
.text-sm, .paragraph-small {
  font-weight: 300;
  font-size: 14px;
  line-height: 140%;
  letter-spacing: -0.03em;
  color: #545658;
}

/* Paragraph Extra Small */
.text-xs, .paragraph-xs {
  font-weight: 400;
  font-size: 13px;
  line-height: 140%;
  letter-spacing: -0.03em;
  color: #545658;
}

.mdx-content li {
  font-family: "GT Standard", sans-serif;
  font-weight: 300;
  font-size: 16px;
  line-height: 140%;
  letter-spacing: -0.03em;
  color: #545658;
}

.dark .mdx-content li {
  color: #ABB0B3;
}

/* Paragraph Styles - Dark Mode */
.dark p,
.dark .prose [data-as="p"],
.dark .prose span[data-as="p"] {
  color: #ABB0B3;
}

.dark .text-lg, .dark .paragraph-large {
  color: #ABB0B3;
}

.dark .text-sm, .dark .paragraph-small {
  color: #ABB0B3;
}

.dark .text-xs, .dark .paragraph-xs {
  color: #ABB0B3;
}

/* Link Styles */
/* Paragraph Link - Light Mode */
/* Apply underline to content links only */
main a,
.content a,
article a,
p a,
li a {
  font-family: "GT Standard", sans-serif;
  font-weight: 400;
  text-decoration: underline;
  color: rgba(18, 21, 22, 0.6);
  transition: color 0.2s ease;
}

main a:hover,
.content a:hover,
article a:hover,
p a:hover,
li a:hover {
  color: #121516;
}

/* Paragraph Link - Dark Mode */
.dark main a,
.dark .content a,
.dark article a,
.dark p a,
.dark li a {
  color: rgba(247, 247, 248, 0.6);
}

/* The cookbook gallery (index) is an interactive component with no exportable
   Markdown, so the built-in "Copy page / View as Markdown" menu does nothing useful
   there. Key off Mintlify's own data-current-path (set on the first frame) so the menu
   is hidden before paint — a JS-toggled class only hides it after hydration, which flashes. */
html[data-current-path="/docs/cookbook"] #page-context-menu {
  display: none !important;
}

/* Cookbook quick-fill chip hover (visible in both themes, unlike the near-invisible card bg). */
.cb-chip:hover {
  background-color: var(--cb-hover);
}

.dark main a:hover,
.dark .content a:hover,
.dark article a:hover,
.dark p a:hover,
.dark li a:hover {
  color: #F7F7F8;
}

/* Small Link - Dark Mode (muted) */
.dark .text-sm a, 
.dark .paragraph-small a {
  color: #ABB0B3;
}

.dark .text-sm a:hover, 
.dark .paragraph-small a:hover {
  color: #F7F7F8;
}

p a,
li a,
span a,
a.link,
[data-component-part="callout-content"] a,
[data-component-part="step-content"] a,
[data-component-part="card-content"] a {
  border-bottom: none !important;
  text-decoration: underline !important;
  text-decoration-thickness: 1px !important;
  text-underline-offset: 2px !important;
}

/* Model cards — restore full border suppressed by the p a rule above */
a.model-card-link {
  border-bottom-width: 1px !important;
  border-bottom-style: solid !important;
  border-bottom-color: var(--color-border) !important;
  text-decoration: none !important;
}

a.model-card-link:hover {
  border-bottom-color: var(--color-primary) !important;
}

/* Ensure sidebar links have no underline */
.almond-layout .sidebar-group a,
.almond-layout a,
#navbar a {
  text-decoration: none !important;
}

/* Always underline inline content links. The broad `.almond-layout a` reset above
   (meant for the sidebar/nav) also matches the content column and, at equal specificity,
   wins by source order over the generic link rules - stripping underlines from real
   prose links. Re-assert underline scoped to #content-area so the ID specificity wins.
   Whole-anchor cards, pagination, heading permalinks, and footer links carry none of
   these selectors, so they stay underline-free. */
#content-area a.link,
#content-area p a,
#content-area li a,
#content-area td a,
#content-area [data-component-part="callout-content"] a,
#content-area [data-component-part="step-content"] a,
#content-area [data-component-part="card-content"] a {
  text-decoration: underline !important;
  text-decoration-thickness: 1px !important;
  text-underline-offset: 2px !important;
}

/* Navbar CTA button */
#topbar-cta-button a,
#topbar-cta-button a span {
  font-family: "GT Standard", sans-serif !important;
  font-weight: 500 !important;
  color: #F7F7F8 !important;
}

#topbar-cta-button a {
  background-color: #1a6872 !important;
}

/* Breathing room from the right edge so the filled button isn't jammed in the
   corner (28px navbar gutter + 36px = ~64px gap). */
#topbar-cta-button {
  margin-right: 36px !important;
}

/* Dark mode: same teal as light mode */
.dark #topbar-cta-button a {
  background-color: #1a6872 !important;
}

/* Far-right placement is handled in navbar-cta.js (the centered tab cluster's
   transform traps positioned children, so the button is relocated in the DOM). */

/* Code Styles */
/* Inline Code - Light Mode */
code {
  font-family: "GT Standard Mono", ui-monospace, SFMono-Regular, Menlo, Monaco, Consolas, monospace;
  font-weight: 400;
  font-size: 13px;
  line-height: 18px;
  letter-spacing: -0.02em;
  color: #545658 !important;
  background-color: rgba(18, 21, 22, 0.04) !important;

}

/* Inline Code - Dark Mode */
.dark code {
  color: #F7F7F8 !important;

}

/* ===========================================
   Standardized Button Styles (Figma Design)
   =========================================== */

/* Default Button - Light Mode */
.btn-default {
  background-color: #121516;
  color: #F7F7F8;
  border-radius: 9999px;
  padding: 0.75rem 1.5rem;
  font-weight: 500;
  font-size: 1rem;
  text-align: center;
  white-space: nowrap;
  transition: all 0.2s ease;
  display: inline-block;
  text-decoration: none;
  border: none;
  cursor: pointer;
}

.btn-default:hover {
  background-color: #0b0c0d;
}

/* Default Button - Dark Mode */
.dark .btn-default {
  background-color: #F7F7F8;
  color: #121516;
}

.dark .btn-default:hover {
  background-color: #FFFFFF;
}

/* Outline Button - Light Mode (blackish) */
.btn-outline {
  background-color: transparent;
  color: #121516;
  border: 2px solid #121516;
  border-radius: 9999px;
  padding: 0.75rem 1.5rem;
  font-weight: 500;
  font-size: 1rem;
  text-align: center;
  white-space: nowrap;
  transition: all 0.2s ease;
  display: inline-block;
  text-decoration: none;
  cursor: pointer;
}

.btn-outline:hover {
  background-color: rgba(18, 21, 22, 0.06);
}

/* Outline Button - Dark Mode */
.dark .btn-outline {
  color: #F7F7F8;
  border-color: #F7F7F8;
}

.dark .btn-outline:hover {
  background-color: rgba(247, 247, 248, 0.14);
}

.dark {
  .bg-dark-turquoise {
    background-color: var(--color-dark-turquoise-dark);
  }
}

/* Code-group wrappers inherit Mintlify's text color utilities. Keep these
   presentation styles scoped to code groups so the same utilities can be used
   by controls such as the search input without adding padding or rounding. */
.code-group.dark\:text-gray-50:is(.dark *) {
  background: rgba(8, 31, 34, 0.3);
  border-radius: 12px;
  padding: 1rem;
}

.code-group.text-gray-950 {

}

/* Remove CodeGroup margins and border in UseCaseTabs */
[id^="usecase-panel-"] .code-group {
  margin: 0 !important;
  border: none !important;
}

/* ===========================================
   Top Navigation - Centered Tabs
   =========================================== */

/* Target the flex container that holds the tabs and center them */
/* Figma shows: left-[calc(50%+92px)] - centered relative to content area, not viewport */
#navbar .ml-auto {
  margin-left: 0 !important;
  position: absolute !important;
  left: calc(50% + 92px) !important;
  transform: translateX(-50%) !important;
  width: auto !important;
  flex: none !important;
}

/* Ensure the nav-tabs container is properly styled with 32px gap (from Figma) */
#navbar .nav-tabs {
  display: flex !important;
  gap: 24px !important;
  align-items: center !important;
}

/* Style individual tab items with pill design - exact Figma specs */
.nav-tabs-item {
  display: flex !important;
  padding: 10px 30px !important;
  justify-content: center !important;
  align-items: center !important;
  gap: 10px !important;
  font-family: "GT Standard", sans-serif !important;
  font-size: 13px !important;
  font-weight: 400 !important;
  letter-spacing: -0.52px !important;
  line-height: normal !important;
  border-radius: 100px !important;

}

/* Active tab pill background - Light mode */
.nav-tabs-item.text-gray-800 {
  background-color: rgba(18, 21, 22, 0.06) !important;
}

/* Active tab pill background - Dark mode */
.dark .nav-tabs-item.dark\:text-gray-200 {

/* Hover state for inactive tabs - Light mode */

}

/* Hover state for inactive tabs - Dark mode */

  background-color: rgba(247, 247, 248, 0.08) !important;
}

/* Remove the default underline indicator */

/* ===========================================
   Callout / Alert Styles (from Figma Design)
   =========================================== */

/* ----------------------------------------
   Base Callout Styles (Universal Attributes)
   - padding: 16px 24px 16px 16px
   - border-radius: 12px
   - border: 1px solid
   - gap (icon + text): 12px
   - icon bounding box: 24px, stroke: 1px
   - font: GT Standard, S Light, 14px, -2% spacing, 140% line-height
   - paragraph spacing: 12px
   ---------------------------------------- */

.callout {
  padding: 16px 24px 16px 16px !important;
  border-radius: 12px !important;
  border-width: 1px !important;
  border-style: solid !important;
  gap: 12px !important;
  overflow: visible !important;
}

/* Callout icon - use default Mintlify sizing */
.callout [data-component-part="callout-icon"] {
  margin-top: 0 !important;
}

/* Callout content typography */
.callout [data-component-part="callout-content"] {
  font-family: "GT Standard", sans-serif !important;
  font-weight: 300 !important;
  font-size: 14px !important;
  letter-spacing: -0.02em !important;
  line-height: 140% !important;
}

.callout [data-component-part="callout-content"] p,
.callout [data-component-part="callout-content"] [data-as="p"] {
  margin-bottom: 12px !important;
}

.callout [data-component-part="callout-content"] p:last-child,
.callout [data-component-part="callout-content"] [data-as="p"]:last-child {
  margin-bottom: 0 !important;
}

/* ----------------------------------------
   Note (blue) — Light Mode
   bg: rgba(66,145,210,0.1)  border: rgba(66,145,210,0.14)  text: #135B8C
   Note — Dark Mode
   bg: rgba(66,145,210,0.18)  border: rgba(66,145,210,0.18)  text: #63AEF2
   ---------------------------------------- */

.callout[data-callout-type="note"] {
  background-color: rgba(66, 145, 210, 0.1) !important;
  border-color: rgba(66, 145, 210, 0.14) !important;
}

.callout[data-callout-type="note"] [data-component-part="callout-icon"] svg {
  color: #135B8C !important;
}

.callout[data-callout-type="note"] [data-component-part="callout-content"] {
  color: #135B8C !important;
}

.dark .callout[data-callout-type="note"] {
  background-color: rgba(66, 145, 210, 0.18) !important;
  border-color: rgba(66, 145, 210, 0.18) !important;
}

.dark .callout[data-callout-type="note"] [data-component-part="callout-icon"] svg {
  color: #63AEF2 !important;
}

.dark .callout[data-callout-type="note"] [data-component-part="callout-content"] {
  color: #63AEF2 !important;
}

/* ----------------------------------------
   Info (neutral gray) — Light Mode
   bg: rgba(18,21,22,0.06)  border: rgba(18,21,22,0.1)  text: #545658
   Info — Dark Mode
   bg: rgba(247,247,248,0.1)  border: rgba(247,247,248,0.14)  text: #ABB0B3
   ---------------------------------------- */

.callout[data-callout-type="info"] {
  background-color: rgba(18, 21, 22, 0.06) !important;
  border-color: rgba(18, 21, 22, 0.1) !important;
}

.callout[data-callout-type="info"] [data-component-part="callout-icon"] svg {

}

.callout[data-callout-type="info"] [data-component-part="callout-content"] {

}

.dark .callout[data-callout-type="info"] {
  background-color: rgba(247, 247, 248, 0.1) !important;

}

.dark .callout[data-callout-type="info"] [data-component-part="callout-icon"] svg {

.dark .callout[data-callout-type="info"] [data-component-part="callout-content"] {

   Tip — Dark Mode
   bg: rgba(75,158,79,0.18)  border: rgba(75,158,79,0.22)  text: #88BB8C
   ---------------------------------------- */

.callout[data-callout-type="tip"] {

/* ===========================================
   Steps Component Styles (from Figma Design)
   =========================================== */

/* ----------------------------------------
   Universal Attributes:
   - numbered text style = H6
   - sub-item text style = Paragraph Regular
   - circled number size = 36px round
   - vertical gap between title and content = 24px
   - vertical gap between items = 48px
   - vertical gap between thread and circle = 8px
   - horizontal gap between circle and item = 20px

   Light Mode:
   - circle bg: rgba(18, 21, 22, 0.06)
   - thread: 1px solid rgba(18, 21, 22, 0.1)

   Dark Mode:
   - circle bg: rgba(247, 247, 248, 0.1)
   - thread: 1px solid rgba(247, 247, 248, 0.1)
   ---------------------------------------- */

/* Steps container — left margin = half circle (18px) */
.steps {
  margin-left: 18px !important;
}

/* Step item — 48px gap between items */
.step-container {
  padding-bottom: 48px !important;
}

.step-container:last-child {
  padding-bottom: 0 !important;
}

/* Step line (thread) — 1px solid, starts 8px below circle */
[data-component-part="step-line"] {
  width: 1px !important;
  left: 0 !important;
  top: 44px !important; /* 36px circle + 8px gap */
  height: calc(100% - 52px) !important;
  background: rgba(18, 21, 22, 0.1) !important;
  background-image: none !important;
}

.dark [data-component-part="step-line"] {
  background: rgba(247, 247, 248, 0.1) !important;
}

/* Step number outer container — center circle on thread */
[data-component-part="step-number"] {
  margin-left: -18px !important;
  padding-top: 0 !important;
  padding-bottom: 0 !important;
}

/* Step number circle — 36px round, H6 text */
[data-component-part="step-number"] > div:first-child {
  width: 36px !important;
  height: 36px !important;
  min-width: 36px !important;
  min-height: 36px !important;
  border-radius: 50% !important;
  background-color: rgba(18, 21, 22, 0.06) !important;
  font-family: "GT Standard", sans-serif !important;
  font-weight: 500 !important;
  font-size: 15px !important;
  line-height: 17px !important;
  letter-spacing: -0.02em !important;
  color: #121516 !important;
}

.dark [data-component-part="step-number"] > div:first-child {
  background-color: rgba(247, 247, 248, 0.1) !important;
  color: #F7F7F8 !important;
}

/* Step content area — 20px gap from circle right edge */
.step-container > .w-full {
  padding-left: 38px !important; /* 18px half-circle + 20px gap */
}

/* Step title — H5 style, vertically centered with 36px circle */
[data-component-part="step-title"] {
  font-family: "GT Standard", sans-serif !important;
  font-weight: 500 !important;
  font-size: 17px !important;
  line-height: 22px !important;
  letter-spacing: -0.02em !important;
  color: #121516 !important;
  margin-top: 7px !important; /* (36 - 22) / 2 = 7px to center */
}

.dark [data-component-part="step-title"] {
  color: #F7F7F8 !important;
}

/* Step content — Paragraph Regular, 24px below title */
[data-component-part="step-content"] {
  margin-top: 24px !important;
}

[data-component-part="step-content"] > p,
[data-component-part="step-content"] > [data-as="p"] {
  font-family: "GT Standard", sans-serif !important;
  font-weight: 300 !important;
  font-size: 16px !important;
  line-height: 140% !important;
  letter-spacing: -0.02em !important;
  color: #545658 !important;
}

.dark [data-component-part="step-content"] > p,
.dark [data-component-part="step-content"] > [data-as="p"] {
  color: #ABB0B3 !important;
}

   Section Menu / Table of Contents (from Figma Design)
   =========================================== */

/* ----------------------------------------
   Desktop TOC (right sidebar — from Figma)

   - Icon (24px) at top, no "On this page" text
   - Vertical 1px thread line alongside links
   - Active item: bright text + bright thread segment
   - Inactive depth-0: 60% opacity
   - Sub-items depth-1+: 50% opacity, indented 20px

/* ----------------------------------------

   ---------------------------------------- */

/* Button — fixed, top-right (from Figma)
   Light: fill #F7F7F8, stroke rgba(18,21,22,0.4), icon #121516
   Dark:  fill #121516, stroke rgba(247,247,248,0.4), icon #F7F7F8

#section-menu-btn {

}

.dark #section-menu-btn svg {

/* Backdrop — invisible overlay to close dropdown on outside click */
#section-menu-backdrop {

/* Dropdown panel (from Figma 202:1395)

#section-menu-dropdown.open {

.dark #section-menu-dropdown {

/* Table wrapper — keep inline with content, don't overflow */
[data-table-wrapper="true"] {
  width: 100% !important;
  max-width: 100% !important;
  margin-left: 0 !important;
  margin-right: 0 !important;
  padding-left: 0 !important;
  padding-right: 0 !important;
}

/* Wide tables scroll horizontally (Mintlify sets overflow-x:auto on this wrapper). macOS/iOS
   hide the overlay scrollbar until you scroll or hover, so a wide table gives no affordance.
   Force a persistent, non-overlay bar. It only renders when a table actually overflows its
   column, so tables that fit are unaffected.
   NB: in Chrome, setting scrollbar-width/color DISABLES ::-webkit-scrollbar and leaves an
   overlay bar (verified: it takes 0 layout height). So Chrome/Safari are styled via the
   pseudo-elements (no scrollbar-width here); Firefox — which ignores the pseudo-elements — is
   handled in the @supports block below. */
[data-table-wrapper="true"]::-webkit-scrollbar {
  height: 8px;
  -webkit-appearance: none;                                /* macOS: classic bar, not overlay */
}
[data-table-wrapper="true"]::-webkit-scrollbar-track {
  background: transparent;
}
[data-table-wrapper="true"]::-webkit-scrollbar-thumb {
  background-color: rgba(18, 21, 22, 0.35);
  border-radius: 4px;
}
[data-table-wrapper="true"]:hover::-webkit-scrollbar-thumb {
  background-color: rgba(18, 21, 22, 0.55);
}
.dark [data-table-wrapper="true"]::-webkit-scrollbar-thumb {
  background-color: rgba(247, 247, 248, 0.35);
}
.dark [data-table-wrapper="true"]:hover::-webkit-scrollbar-thumb {
  background-color: rgba(247, 247, 248, 0.55);
}
/* Firefox: no ::-webkit-scrollbar support — use the standard properties (persistent once colored). */
@supports not (selector(::-webkit-scrollbar)) {
  [data-table-wrapper="true"] {
    scrollbar-width: thin;
    scrollbar-color: rgba(18, 21, 22, 0.35) transparent;
  }
  .dark [data-table-wrapper="true"] {
    scrollbar-color: rgba(247, 247, 248, 0.35) transparent;
  }
}

/* Table base — clean borders */

/* Code in table cells — keep mono font, inherit size */
.table td code {
  font-size: 13px !important;
  padding: 2px 6px !important;
}

/* First column: keep code identifiers from breaking */
.table td:first-child code {
  white-space: nowrap;
}

/* Header cells: never wrap */
.table th {
  white-space: nowrap;
}

/* Type column: allow wrapping */
.table td:nth-child(2) {
  white-space: normal;
  word-break: break-word;
}

/* Links in table cells — match normal content links (underline + link color + hover) */
.table td a {
  color: rgba(18, 21, 22, 0.6) !important;
  text-decoration: underline !important;
  text-decoration-thickness: 1px !important;
  text-underline-offset: 2px !important;
  transition: color 0.2s ease;
}

.table td a:hover {
  color: #121516 !important;
}

.dark .table td a {
  color: rgba(247, 247, 248, 0.6) !important;
}

.dark .table td a:hover {
  color: #F7F7F8 !important;
}

/* ===========================================
   Sidebar Styles (from Figma Design)
   =========================================== */

/* ----------------------------------------
   Menu Headers
   - text color = #F7F7F8 (dark) / #121516 (light)
   - font size = 13px
   - font family = GT Standard
   - font weight = S Semibold (600)
   - letter spacing = -2% (-0.02em)
   ---------------------------------------- */

.sidebar-group-header {
  font-size: 13px !important;
  font-family: "GT Standard", sans-serif !important;
  font-weight: 600 !important;
  letter-spacing: -0.02em !important;
  text-transform: none !important;
  color: #121516 !important;
}

.dark .sidebar-group-header {
  color: #F7F7F8 !important;
}

/* ----------------------------------------
   Menu Links (plain links AND expandable group rows)
   - default link color = #121516 (light) / #F7F7F8 (dark) — matches group headers
   - active link color = rgba(247, 247, 248, 1)
   - active link bg color = rgba(247, 247, 248, 0.14)
   - active link padding = 6px 10px
   - active link corner radius = 8px
   - text style = 13px, 400, 140%, -0.02em
   ---------------------------------------- */

/* Default sidebar links - text styling only, no layout changes.
   Color matches the group headers (full-opacity) so non-group links no
   longer read as muted/grey; the expand chevron remains the only group cue.
   Expandable group rows render as <button aria-expanded> (not <a>), so they
   are included here to share the same full-opacity color in both themes. */
.sidebar-group a,
.sidebar-group button[aria-expanded] {
  font-size: 13px !important;
  font-family: "GT Standard", sans-serif !important;
  font-weight: 400 !important;
  line-height: 140% !important;
  letter-spacing: -0.02em !important;
  text-decoration: none !important;
  color: #121516 !important;
  transition: background-color 0.15s ease, color 0.15s ease !important;
}

.dark .sidebar-group a,
.dark .sidebar-group button[aria-expanded] {
  color: #F7F7F8 !important;
}

/* Active sidebar links */
.sidebar-group a.bg-primary\/10,
.sidebar-group a[aria-current="page"] {
  background: rgba(18, 21, 22, 0.06) !important;
  color: rgba(18, 21, 22, 1) !important;
  border-radius: 8px !important;
}

.dark .sidebar-group a.bg-primary\/10,
.dark .sidebar-group a[aria-current="page"] {
  background: rgba(247, 247, 248, 0.14) !important;
  color: rgba(247, 247, 248, 1) !important;
}

/* Hover sidebar links and expandable group rows */
.sidebar-group a:hover,
.sidebar-group button[aria-expanded]:hover {
  background: rgba(18, 21, 22, 0.06) !important;
  color: rgba(18, 21, 22, 1) !important;
  border-radius: 8px !important;
}

.dark .sidebar-group a:hover,
.dark .sidebar-group button[aria-expanded]:hover {
  background: rgba(247, 247, 248, 0.14) !important;
  color: rgba(247, 247, 248, 1) !important;
}

/* ----------------------------------------
   Sidebar Icons
   - icon weight = 1px stroke
   - icon (bounding box) size = 16px
   - icon color = rgba(247, 247, 248, 0.6)
   ---------------------------------------- */

.sidebar-group svg {
  width: 16px !important;
  height: 16px !important;
  stroke-width: 1px !important;
  color: rgba(18, 21, 22, 0.6) !important;
}

.dark .sidebar-group svg {
  color: rgba(247, 247, 248, 0.6) !important;
}

/* Icons in active/hover state */
.sidebar-group a.bg-primary\/10 svg,
.sidebar-group a[aria-current="page"] svg,
.sidebar-group a:hover svg,
.sidebar-group button[aria-expanded]:hover svg {
  color: rgba(18, 21, 22, 1) !important;
}

.dark .sidebar-group a.bg-primary\/10 svg,
.dark .sidebar-group a[aria-current="page"] svg,
.dark .sidebar-group a:hover svg,
.dark .sidebar-group button[aria-expanded]:hover svg {
  color: rgba(247, 247, 248, 1) !important;
}

/* Cookbook gallery cards render inside content, where Mintlify underlines every
   in-content link (a.link / #content-area li a). Keep the whole card clean; the
   title still gets its own underline on hover via group-hover:underline. */

<span class="line"><span>        "content": "Magnetic confinement fusion uses strong magnetic fields to trap a very hot, ionized gas (plasma) so that light nuclei collide and fuse faster than the energy is lost, and the Lawson criterion quantifies the minimum combination of plasma density, temperature, and confinement time required for this to produce net energy. The core physics is charged-particle motion in magnetic fields (guiding centers following field lines plus gyration and drifts), collective plasma stability, and energy balance; the Lawson criterion is the formal expression of that energy balance.\n\n---\n\n### 1. Why fusion needs confinement\n\nFor deuterium–tritium (D–T) fusion to occur at an appreciable rate, the plasma must reach temperatures of order \\(10^8\\) K (∼10 keV), hotter than the Sun’s core, so that nuclei can overcome the Coulomb repulsion and get close enough for the strong nuclear force to fuse them.[1][4][6] At these temperatures:\n\n- All atoms are ionized → a **plasma** of electrons and ions.[1][4][6]  \n- No solid material can touch the plasma; it would vaporize instantly.[1][4]\n\nSo fusion requires:\n\n- **Heating** the fuel to fusion temperatures.  \n- **Confining** it long enough and dense enough that many fusion reactions occur before the energy escapes.[4][6]\n\nIn stars, gravity provides confinement; in labs, strong magnetic fields are used instead.[4][6]\n\n---\n\n### 2. Single-particle motion: how magnetic fields confine charges\n\nThe basic building block is the Lorentz force on a charged particle in a magnetic field: \\(\\mathbf{F} = q\\,\\mathbf{v} \\times \\mathbf{B}\\).\n\nFrom this follow key motions (as shown in standard plasma-physics treatments and educational material):[2][3][6]\n\n- A component of velocity **perpendicular** to \\(\\mathbf{B}\\) causes **circular gyro-motion** around the field line at the Larmor radius.  \n- A component **parallel** to \\(\\mathbf{B}\\) feels no magnetic force and moves freely along the field.[2]  \n\nCombined, ions and electrons **spiral** along magnetic field lines: they are tightly bound across the field but free to move along it.[2][3][6]\n\nThis leads to the confinement idea:\n\n- Shape the magnetic field so that **field lines are closed** (e.g., in a torus), forming a “magnetic bottle.”  \n- Particles spiral around these closed lines, remaining away from material walls.[1][3][6]\n\nThe stronger the magnetic field:\n\n- The **smaller** the Larmor radius.  \n- The **slower** cross-field drifts and diffusion.  \n- The **better** the confinement.[2][3]\n\n---\n\n### 3. From single particles to plasma: collective and MHD behavior\n\nAt fusion-relevant densities, the plasma’s own currents and charges significantly modify the externally applied magnetic field, and the medium must be treated collectively.[2][3][7] This is described by **magnetohydrodynamics (MHD)**:\n\n- The plasma behaves like a conducting fluid embedded in magnetic field lines.  \n- Magnetic field lines are often described as “frozen in” to the plasma: fluid elements move along field lines, and dragging the plasma across the field tends to drag the lines with it.[2]\n\nKey implications for magnetic confinement:\n\n- **Pressure balance:** Plasma pressure pushes outward, magnetic pressure and tension pull inward. Stable confinement demands that the magnetic field be strong enough and appropriately shaped to counter plasma pressure and currents.[3][7]  \n- **Instabilities:** Certain pressure/current configurations are unstable (e.g., kink, ballooning, interchange instabilities), leading to bulging, twisting, or breaking of confined regions and degraded confinement.[2][3][6][7]  \n- **Turbulence:** Small-scale fluctuations and turbulence cause enhanced transport of heat and particles across field lines, reducing the effective confinement time below what classical single-particle theory would predict.[2][3][7]\n\nDesigning a successful magnetic confinement system is largely about **finding magnetic geometries and operating regimes that avoid or tame these instabilities** and minimize turbulent transport.[3][6][7]\n\n---\n\n### 4. Magnetic geometry in practice: toroidal devices\n\nBecause particles stream freely along field lines, the field lines themselves must not intersect walls, which leads naturally to **toroidal (doughnut-shaped)** configurations:[1][5][6]\n\n- **Tokamak:**  \n  - Strong toroidal field from external coils.  \n  - Large plasma current generates a poloidal field, twisting field lines into helical paths, improving confinement and stability.[5][6][7]  \n- **Stellarator:**  \n  - Uses 3D-shaped external coils to create the required helical fields; does not rely on a large plasma current, which avoids some current-driven instabilities but demands complex coil engineering.[5][6][7]\n\nTwist in the field lines helps cancel or average out systematic drifts that would otherwise move particles to the wall.[2][6]\n\nOther configurations (mirror machines, reversed-field pinches, spherical tokamaks, etc.) explore different ways of shaping \\(\\mathbf{B}\\), but modern mainstream MCF focuses on tokamaks and stellarators.[5][6][7]\n\n---\n\n### 5. Energy balance and the Lawson criterion\n\nTo generate net power, the fusion plasma must satisfy an **energy balance condition**: fusion power produced must equal or exceed total power lost (radiation, conduction, convection, particle escape).[6][7]\n\nFor a D–T plasma, this condition is commonly expressed as the **Lawson criterion**, which relates:\n\n- **n** – plasma particle density  \n- **T** – temperature  \n- **τ\\_E** – energy confinement time (a measure of how long energy stays in the plasma before being lost)\n\nIn one common form, the Lawson criterion requires that the **triple product** \\(n T \\tau_E\\) exceed a critical value for ignition (self-sustaining fusion without external heating) or for net energy gain.[6][7]\n\nConceptually:\n\n- Fusion power density \\(\\propto n^2 \\langle \\sigma v \\rangle\\), where \\(\\langle \\sigma v \\rangle\\) increases with temperature up to an optimum.  \n- Loss power density \\(\\propto \\frac{3 n T}{\\tau_E}\\) (roughly, energy per particle divided by confinement time).  \n- Setting fusion power ≥ loss power gives a condition on \\(n T \\tau_E\\).[6][7]\n\nFor D–T at ∼10–20 keV, the required triple product is on the order of \\(10^{21}\\,\\text{keV·s·m}^{-3}\\) (order-of-magnitude; exact numbers depend on detailed assumptions), and modern large tokamaks operate near or approaching this regime in brief pulses.[6][7]\n\n**Role of the Lawson criterion in MCF:**\n\n- It defines the **minimum combination** of density, temperature, and confinement time needed for practical fusion.  \n- Because the temperature window is fairly constrained by fusion cross sections, MCF devices mostly trade off **density versus confinement time**:  \n  - Magnetic confinement operates at relatively **low density** and **long τ\\_E** (milliseconds to seconds or longer).  \n  - Inertial confinement operates at very **high density** and extremely **short τ\\_E** (nanoseconds).  \n- It provides a quantitative **performance metric**: experiments report their achieved \\(n T \\tau_E\\) and compare to the Lawson threshold for ignition or for specific gain factors.[6][7]\n\nIn short, the Lawson criterion translates “good enough confinement” into a precise inequality involving measurable plasma parameters.\n\n---\n\n### 6. Why magnetic confinement is hard\n\nLinking the physics pieces:\n\n- **Single-particle physics** explains why strong magnetic fields can, in principle, confine hot plasmas away from walls.  \n- **Collective and MHD physics** explain why real plasmas develop currents, instabilities, and turbulence that degrade that ideal confinement.  \n- The **Lawson criterion** states the quantitative target: despite all losses, achieve a triple product high enough that fusion heating balances or exceeds losses.\n\nMajor technical and physics challenges in MCF include:[3][4][6][7]\n\n- Achieving and sustaining **multi-tesla magnetic fields** with high precision.  \n- Controlling **MHD instabilities** and turbulent transport to attain long τ\\_E.  \n- Handling **extreme heat and particle loads** where confined plasma meets material surfaces (divertors, first wall).[3]  \n- Integrating materials, superconducting magnets, heating systems, and control systems to operate reliably for long durations.[3][6][7]\n\nAll of these are pursued with the Lawson criterion in mind: improving confinement time and allowable density at a given temperature to reach or surpass the ignition and net-gain conditions.\n\nIf you’d like, I can next walk through the Lawson criterion derivation step-by-step from the energy balance equations, or compare typical Lawson targets for magnetic vs inertial confinement.",</span></span>

<span class="line"><span>        "content": "Magnetic confinement fusion uses strong magnetic fields to trap a very hot, ionized gas (plasma) so that light nuclei collide and fuse faster than the energy is lost, and the Lawson criterion quantifies the minimum combination of plasma density, temperature, and confinement time required for this to produce net energy. The core physics is charged-particle motion in magnetic fields (guiding centers following field lines plus gyration and drifts), collective plasma stability, and energy balance; the Lawson criterion is the formal expression of that energy balance.\n\n---\n\n### 1. Why fusion needs confinement\n\nFor deuterium–tritium (D–T) fusion to occur at an appreciable rate, the plasma must reach temperatures of order \\(10^8\\) K (∼10 keV), hotter than the Sun’s core, so that nuclei can overcome the Coulomb repulsion and get close enough for the strong nuclear force to fuse them.[1][4][6] At these temperatures:\n\n- All atoms are ionized → a **plasma** of electrons and ions.[1][4][6]  \n- No solid material can touch the plasma; it would vaporize instantly.[1][4]\n\nSo fusion requires:\n\n- **Heating** the fuel to fusion temperatures.  \n- **Confining** it long enough and dense enough that many fusion reactions occur before the energy escapes.[4][6]\n\nIn stars, gravity provides confinement; in labs, strong magnetic fields are used instead.[4][6]\n\n---\n\n### 2. Single-particle motion: how magnetic fields confine charges\n\nThe basic building block is the Lorentz force on a charged particle in a magnetic field: \\(\\mathbf{F} = q\\,\\mathbf{v} \\times \\mathbf{B}\\).\n\nFrom this follow key motions (as shown in standard plasma-physics treatments and educational material):[2][3][6]\n\n- A component of velocity **perpendicular** to \\(\\mathbf{B}\\) causes **circular gyro-motion** around the field line at the Larmor radius.  \n- A component **parallel** to \\(\\mathbf{B}\\) feels no magnetic force and moves freely along the field.[2]  \n\nCombined, ions and electrons **spiral** along magnetic field lines: they are tightly bound across the field but free to move along it.[2][3][6]\n\nThis leads to the confinement idea:\n\n- Shape the magnetic field so that **field lines are closed** (e.g., in a torus), forming a “magnetic bottle.”  \n- Particles spiral around these closed lines, remaining away from material walls.[1][3][6]\n\nThe stronger the magnetic field:\n\n- The **smaller** the Larmor radius.  \n- The **slower** cross-field drifts and diffusion.  \n- The **better** the confinement.[2][3]\n\n---\n\n### 3. From single particles to plasma: collective and MHD behavior\n\nAt fusion-relevant densities, the plasma’s own currents and charges significantly modify the externally applied magnetic field, and the medium must be treated collectively.[2][3][7] This is described by **magnetohydrodynamics (MHD)**:\n\n- The plasma behaves like a conducting fluid embedded in magnetic field lines.  \n- Magnetic field lines are often described as “frozen in” to the plasma: fluid elements move along field lines, and dragging the plasma across the field tends to drag the lines with it.[2]\n\nKey implications for magnetic confinement:\n\n- **Pressure balance:** Plasma pressure pushes outward, magnetic pressure and tension pull inward. Stable confinement demands that the magnetic field be strong enough and appropriately shaped to counter plasma pressure and currents.[3][7]  \n- **Instabilities:** Certain pressure/current configurations are unstable (e.g., kink, ballooning, interchange instabilities), leading to bulging, twisting, or breaking of confined regions and degraded confinement.[2][3][6][7]  \n- **Turbulence:** Small-scale fluctuations and turbulence cause enhanced transport of heat and particles across field lines, reducing the effective confinement time below what classical single-particle theory would predict.[2][3][7]\n\nDesigning a successful magnetic confinement system is largely about **finding magnetic geometries and operating regimes that avoid or tame these instabilities** and minimize turbulent transport.[3][6][7]\n\n---\n\n### 4. Magnetic geometry in practice: toroidal devices\n\nBecause particles stream freely along field lines, the field lines themselves must not intersect walls, which leads naturally to **toroidal (doughnut-shaped)** configurations:[1][5][6]\n\n- **Tokamak:**  \n  - Strong toroidal field from external coils.  \n  - Large plasma current generates a poloidal field, twisting field lines into helical paths, improving confinement and stability.[5][6][7]  \n- **Stellarator:**  \n  - Uses 3D-shaped external coils to create the required helical fields; does not rely on a large plasma current, which avoids some current-driven instabilities but demands complex coil engineering.[5][6][7]\n\nTwist in the field lines helps cancel or average out systematic drifts that would otherwise move particles to the wall.[2][6]\n\nOther configurations (mirror machines, reversed-field pinches, spherical tokamaks, etc.) explore different ways of shaping \\(\\mathbf{B}\\), but modern mainstream MCF focuses on tokamaks and stellarators.[5][6][7]\n\n---\n\n### 5. Energy balance and the Lawson criterion\n\nTo generate net power, the fusion plasma must satisfy an **energy balance condition**: fusion power produced must equal or exceed total power lost (radiation, conduction, convection, particle escape).[6][7]\n\nFor a D–T plasma, this condition is commonly expressed as the **Lawson criterion**, which relates:\n\n- **n** – plasma particle density  \n- **T** – temperature  \n- **τ\\_E** – energy confinement time (a measure of how long energy stays in the plasma before being lost)\n\nIn one common form, the Lawson criterion requires that the **triple product** \\(n T \\tau_E\\) exceed a critical value for ignition (self-sustaining fusion without external heating) or for net energy gain.[6][7]\n\nConceptually:\n\n- Fusion power density \\(\\propto n^2 \\langle \\sigma v \\rangle\\), where \\(\\langle \\sigma v \\rangle\\) increases with temperature up to an optimum.  \n- Loss power density \\(\\propto \\frac{3 n T}{\\tau_E}\\) (roughly, energy per particle divided by confinement time).  \n- Setting fusion power ≥ loss power gives a condition on \\(n T \\tau_E\\).[6][7]\n\nFor D–T at ∼10–20 keV, the required triple product is on the order of \\(10^{21}\\,\\text{keV·s·m}^{-3}\\) (order-of-magnitude; exact numbers depend on detailed assumptions), and modern large tokamaks operate near or approaching this regime in brief pulses.[6][7]\n\n**Role of the Lawson criterion in MCF:**\n\n- It defines the **minimum combination** of density, temperature, and confinement time needed for practical fusion.  \n- Because the temperature window is fairly constrained by fusion cross sections, MCF devices mostly trade off **density versus confinement time**:  \n  - Magnetic confinement operates at relatively **low density** and **long τ\\_E** (milliseconds to seconds or longer).  \n  - Inertial confinement operates at very **high density** and extremely **short τ\\_E** (nanoseconds).  \n- It provides a quantitative **performance metric**: experiments report their achieved \\(n T \\tau_E\\) and compare to the Lawson threshold for ignition or for specific gain factors.[6][7]\n\nIn short, the Lawson criterion translates “good enough confinement” into a precise inequality involving measurable plasma parameters.\n\n---\n\n### 6. Why magnetic confinement is hard\n\nLinking the physics pieces:\n\n- **Single-particle physics** explains why strong magnetic fields can, in principle, confine hot plasmas away from walls.  \n- **Collective and MHD physics** explain why real plasmas develop currents, instabilities, and turbulence that degrade that ideal confinement.  \n- The **Lawson criterion** states the quantitative target: despite all losses, achieve a triple product high enough that fusion heating balances or exceeds losses.\n\nMajor technical and physics challenges in MCF include:[3][4][6][7]\n\n- Achieving and sustaining **multi-tesla magnetic fields** with high precision.  \n- Controlling **MHD instabilities** and turbulent transport to attain long τ\\_E.  \n- Handling **extreme heat and particle loads** where confined plasma meets material surfaces (divertors, first wall).[3]  \n- Integrating materials, superconducting magnets, heating systems, and control systems to operate reliably for long durations.[3][6][7]\n\nAll of these are pursued with the Lawson criterion in mind: improving confinement time and allowable density at a given temperature to reach or surpass the ignition and net-gain conditions.\n\nIf you’d like, I can next walk through the Lawson criterion derivation step-by-step from the energy balance equations, or compare typical Lawson targets for magnetic vs inertial confinement.",</span></span>

<span class="line"><span>        "content": "Magnetic confinement fusion uses strong magnetic fields to trap a very hot, ionized gas (plasma) so that light nuclei collide and fuse faster than the energy is lost, and the Lawson criterion quantifies the minimum combination of plasma density, temperature, and confinement time required for this to produce net energy. The core physics is charged-particle motion in magnetic fields (guiding centers following field lines plus gyration and drifts), collective plasma stability, and energy balance; the Lawson criterion is the formal expression of that energy balance.\n\n---\n\n### 1. Why fusion needs confinement\n\nFor deuterium–tritium (D–T) fusion to occur at an appreciable rate, the plasma must reach temperatures of order \\(10^8\\) K (∼10 keV), hotter than the Sun’s core, so that nuclei can overcome the Coulomb repulsion and get close enough for the strong nuclear force to fuse them.[1][4][6] At these temperatures:\n\n- All atoms are ionized → a **plasma** of electrons and ions.[1][4][6]  \n- No solid material can touch the plasma; it would vaporize instantly.[1][4]\n\nSo fusion requires:\n\n- **Heating** the fuel to fusion temperatures.  \n- **Confining** it long enough and dense enough that many fusion reactions occur before the energy escapes.[4][6]\n\nIn stars, gravity provides confinement; in labs, strong magnetic fields are used instead.[4][6]\n\n---\n\n### 2. Single-particle motion: how magnetic fields confine charges\n\nThe basic building block is the Lorentz force on a charged particle in a magnetic field: \\(\\mathbf{F} = q\\,\\mathbf{v} \\times \\mathbf{B}\\).\n\nFrom this follow key motions (as shown in standard plasma-physics treatments and educational material):[2][3][6]\n\n- A component of velocity **perpendicular** to \\(\\mathbf{B}\\) causes **circular gyro-motion** around the field line at the Larmor radius.  \n- A component **parallel** to \\(\\mathbf{B}\\) feels no magnetic force and moves freely along the field.[2]  \n\nCombined, ions and electrons **spiral** along magnetic field lines: they are tightly bound across the field but free to move along it.[2][3][6]\n\nThis leads to the confinement idea:\n\n- Shape the magnetic field so that **field lines are closed** (e.g., in a torus), forming a “magnetic bottle.”  \n- Particles spiral around these closed lines, remaining away from material walls.[1][3][6]\n\nThe stronger the magnetic field:\n\n- The **smaller** the Larmor radius.  \n- The **slower** cross-field drifts and diffusion.  \n- The **better** the confinement.[2][3]\n\n---\n\n### 3. From single particles to plasma: collective and MHD behavior\n\nAt fusion-relevant densities, the plasma’s own currents and charges significantly modify the externally applied magnetic field, and the medium must be treated collectively.[2][3][7] This is described by **magnetohydrodynamics (MHD)**:\n\n- The plasma behaves like a conducting fluid embedded in magnetic field lines.  \n- Magnetic field lines are often described as “frozen in” to the plasma: fluid elements move along field lines, and dragging the plasma across the field tends to drag the lines with it.[2]\n\nKey implications for magnetic confinement:\n\n- **Pressure balance:** Plasma pressure pushes outward, magnetic pressure and tension pull inward. Stable confinement demands that the magnetic field be strong enough and appropriately shaped to counter plasma pressure and currents.[3][7]  \n- **Instabilities:** Certain pressure/current configurations are unstable (e.g., kink, ballooning, interchange instabilities), leading to bulging, twisting, or breaking of confined regions and degraded confinement.[2][3][6][7]  \n- **Turbulence:** Small-scale fluctuations and turbulence cause enhanced transport of heat and particles across field lines, reducing the effective confinement time below what classical single-particle theory would predict.[2][3][7]\n\nDesigning a successful magnetic confinement system is largely about **finding magnetic geometries and operating regimes that avoid or tame these instabilities** and minimize turbulent transport.[3][6][7]\n\n---\n\n### 4. Magnetic geometry in practice: toroidal devices\n\nBecause particles stream freely along field lines, the field lines themselves must not intersect walls, which leads naturally to **toroidal (doughnut-shaped)** configurations:[1][5][6]\n\n- **Tokamak:**  \n  - Strong toroidal field from external coils.  \n  - Large plasma current generates a poloidal field, twisting field lines into helical paths, improving confinement and stability.[5][6][7]  \n- **Stellarator:**  \n  - Uses 3D-shaped external coils to create the required helical fields; does not rely on a large plasma current, which avoids some current-driven instabilities but demands complex coil engineering.[5][6][7]\n\nTwist in the field lines helps cancel or average out systematic drifts that would otherwise move particles to the wall.[2][6]\n\nOther configurations (mirror machines, reversed-field pinches, spherical tokamaks, etc.) explore different ways of shaping \\(\\mathbf{B}\\), but modern mainstream MCF focuses on tokamaks and stellarators.[5][6][7]\n\n---\n\n### 5. Energy balance and the Lawson criterion\n\nTo generate net power, the fusion plasma must satisfy an **energy balance condition**: fusion power produced must equal or exceed total power lost (radiation, conduction, convection, particle escape).[6][7]\n\nFor a D–T plasma, this condition is commonly expressed as the **Lawson criterion**, which relates:\n\n- **n** – plasma particle density  \n- **T** – temperature  \n- **τ\\_E** – energy confinement time (a measure of how long energy stays in the plasma before being lost)\n\nIn one common form, the Lawson criterion requires that the **triple product** \\(n T \\tau_E\\) exceed a critical value for ignition (self-sustaining fusion without external heating) or for net energy gain.[6][7]\n\nConceptually:\n\n- Fusion power density \\(\\propto n^2 \\langle \\sigma v \\rangle\\), where \\(\\langle \\sigma v \\rangle\\) increases with temperature up to an optimum.  \n- Loss power density \\(\\propto \\frac{3 n T}{\\tau_E}\\) (roughly, energy per particle divided by confinement time).  \n- Setting fusion power ≥ loss power gives a condition on \\(n T \\tau_E\\).[6][7]\n\nFor D–T at ∼10–20 keV, the required triple product is on the order of \\(10^{21}\\,\\text{keV·s·m}^{-3}\\) (order-of-magnitude; exact numbers depend on detailed assumptions), and modern large tokamaks operate near or approaching this regime in brief pulses.[6][7]\n\n**Role of the Lawson criterion in MCF:**\n\n- It defines the **minimum combination** of density, temperature, and confinement time needed for practical fusion.  \n- Because the temperature window is fairly constrained by fusion cross sections, MCF devices mostly trade off **density versus confinement time**:  \n  - Magnetic confinement operates at relatively **low density** and **long τ\\_E** (milliseconds to seconds or longer).  \n  - Inertial confinement operates at very **high density** and extremely **short τ\\_E** (nanoseconds).  \n- It provides a quantitative **performance metric**: experiments report their achieved \\(n T \\tau_E\\) and compare to the Lawson threshold for ignition or for specific gain factors.[6][7]\n\nIn short, the Lawson criterion translates “good enough confinement” into a precise inequality involving measurable plasma parameters.\n\n---\n\n### 6. Why magnetic confinement is hard\n\nLinking the physics pieces:\n\n- **Single-particle physics** explains why strong magnetic fields can, in principle, confine hot plasmas away from walls.  \n- **Collective and MHD physics** explain why real plasmas develop currents, instabilities, and turbulence that degrade that ideal confinement.  \n- The **Lawson criterion** states the quantitative target: despite all losses, achieve a triple product high enough that fusion heating balances or exceeds losses.\n\nMajor technical and physics challenges in MCF include:[3][4][6][7]\n\n- Achieving and sustaining **multi-tesla magnetic fields** with high precision.  \n- Controlling **MHD instabilities** and turbulent transport to attain long τ\\_E.  \n- Handling **extreme heat and particle loads** where confined plasma meets material surfaces (divertors, first wall).[3]  \n- Integrating materials, superconducting magnets, heating systems, and control systems to operate reliably for long durations.[3][6][7]\n\nAll of these are pursued with the Lawson criterion in mind: improving confinement time and allowable density at a given temperature to reach or surpass the ignition and net-gain conditions.\n\nIf you’d like, I can next walk through the Lawson criterion derivation step-by-step from the energy balance equations, or compare typical Lawson targets for magnetic vs inertial confinement.",</span></span>

<span data-as="p">These parameters work exactly the same as OpenAI’s API:</span>
<ul>
<li><code>model</code> - Model name (use Perplexity model names like <code>sonar-pro</code>)</li>
<li><code>messages</code> - Chat messages array</li>
<li><code>max_tokens</code> - Maximum tokens in response</li>
<li><code>stream</code> - Enable streaming responses</li>
<li><code>temperature</code> - Response randomness (0-2)</li>
<li><code>top_p</code> - Nucleus sampling parameter</li>
<li><code>response_format</code> - Response format specification</li>
</ul>
<h3 class="flex whitespace-pre-wrap group font-semibold" id="perplexity-specific-parameters-2"><div class="absolute" tabindex="-1"><a href="#perplexity-specific-parameters-2" class="-ml-10 flex items-center opacity-0 border-0 group-hover:opacity-100 focus:opacity-100 focus:outline-0 group/link" aria-label="Navigate to header">​<div class="size-6 rounded-md flex items-center justify-center shadow-xs text-gray-400 dark:text-white/50 dark:bg-background-dark dark:brightness-[1.35] dark:ring-1 dark:hover:brightness-150 bg-white ring-1 ring-gray-400/30 dark:ring-gray-700/25 hover:ring-gray-400/60 dark:hover:ring-white/20 group-focus/link:border-2 group-focus/link:border-primary dark:group-focus/link:border-primary-light"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="18" height="18" viewBox="0 0 18 18" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true" class="size-3 shrink-0"><path d="M8.50001 6.827C8.14801 6.995 7.81801 7.225 7.52701 7.517L7.51701 7.527C6.13601 8.908 6.13601 11.146 7.51701 12.527L9.69201 14.702C11.073 16.083 13.311 16.083 14.692 14.702L14.702 14.692C16.083 13.311 16.083 11.073 14.702 9.692L13.771 8.761" stroke="currentColor" width="1.5" linecap="round" linejoin="round"></path><path d="M9.50002 11.173C9.85202 11.005 10.182 10.775 10.473 10.483L10.483 10.473C11.864 9.092 11.864 6.854 10.483 5.473L8.30802 3.298C6.92702 1.917 4.68902 1.917 3.30802 3.298L3.29802 3.308C1.91702 4.689 1.91702 6.927 3.29802 8.308L4.22902 9.239" stroke="currentColor" width="1.5" linecap="round" linejoin="round"></path></svg></div></a></div><span class="cursor-pointer">Perplexity-Specific Parameters</span></h3>
<span data-as="p">Sonar API supports additional search and response parameters:</span>
<ul>
<li><code>search_domain_filter</code> - Limit or exclude specific domains</li>
<li><code>search_recency_filter</code> - Filter by content recency (“day”, “week”, “month”, “year”)</li>
<li><code>return_images</code> - Include image URLs in response</li>
<li><code>return_related_questions</code> - Include related questions</li>
<li><code>search_mode</code> - “web” (default) or “academic” mode selector</li>
<li><code>enable_search_classifier</code> - Let AI decide when to search</li>
<li><code>disable_search</code> - Turn off web search completely</li>
</ul>

<h3 class="flex whitespace-pre-wrap group font-semibold" id="standard-openai-fields"><div class="absolute" tabindex="-1"><a href="#standard-openai-fields" class="-ml-10 flex items-center opacity-0 border-0 group-hover:opacity-100 focus:opacity-100 focus:outline-0 group/link" aria-label="Navigate to header">​<div class="size-6 rounded-md flex items-center justify-center shadow-xs text-gray-400 dark:text-white/50 dark:bg-background-dark dark:brightness-[1.35] dark:ring-1 dark:hover:brightness-150 bg-white ring-1 ring-gray-400/30 dark:ring-gray-700/25 hover:ring-gray-400/60 dark:hover:ring-white/20 group-focus/link:border-2 group-focus/link:border-primary dark:group-focus/link:border-primary-light"><svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="18" height="18" viewBox="0 0 18 18" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" aria-hidden="true" class="size-3 shrink-0"><path d="M8.50001 6.827C8.14801 6.995 7.81801 7.225 7.52701 7.517L7.51701 7.527C6.13601 8.908 6.13601 11.146 7.51701 12.527L9.69201 14.702C11.073 16.083 13.311 16.083 14.692 14.702L14.702 14.692C16.083 13.311 16.083 11.073 14.702 9.692L13.771 8.761" stroke="currentColor" width="1.5" linecap="round" linejoin="round"></path><path d="M9.50002 11.173C9.85202 11.005 10.182 10.775 10.473 10.483L10.483 10.473C11.864 9.092 11.864 6.854 10.483 5.473L8.30802 3.298C6.92702 1.917 4.68902 1.917 3.30802 3.298L3.29802 3.308C1.91702 4.689 1.91702 6.927 3.29802 8.308L4.22902 9.239" stroke="currentColor" width="1.5" linecap="round" linejoin="round"></path></svg></div></a></div><span class="cursor-pointer">Standard OpenAI Fields</span></h3>
<ul>
<li><code>choices[0].message.content</code> - The AI-generated response</li>
<li><code>model</code> - The model name used</li>
<li><code>usage</code> - Token consumption details</li>
<li><code>id</code>, <code>created</code>, <code>object</code> - Standard response metadata</li>
</ul>

</ul>

ionized gas (plasma) so that light nuclei collide and fuse faster than the energy is lost, and the Lawson criterion quantifies the minimum combination of plasma density, temperature, and confinement time required for this to produce net energy. The core physics is charged-particle motion in magnetic fields (guiding centers following field lines plus gyration and drifts), collective plasma stability, and energy balance; the Lawson criterion is the formal expression of that energy balance.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### 1. Why fusion needs confinement\\\\n\\\\nFor deuterium–tritium (D–T) fusion to occur at an appreciable rate, the plasma must reach temperatures of order \\\\\\\\(10^8\\\\\\\\) K (∼10 keV), hotter than the Sun’s core, so that nuclei can overcome the Coulomb repulsion and get close enough for the strong nuclear force to fuse them.[1][4][6] At these temperatures:\\\\n\\\\n- All atoms are ionized → a **plasma** of electrons and ions.[1][4][6]  \\\\n- No solid material can touch the plasma; it would vaporize instantly.[1][4]\\\\n\\\\nSo fusion requires:\\\\n\\\\n- **Heating** the fuel to fusion temperatures.  \\\\n- **Confining** it long enough and dense enough that many fusion reactions occur before the energy escapes.[4][6]\\\\n\\\\nIn stars, gravity provides confinement; in labs, strong magnetic fields are used instead.[4][6]\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### 2. Single-particle motion: how magnetic fields confine charges\\\\n\\\\nThe basic building block is the Lorentz force on a charged particle in a magnetic field: \\\\\\\\(\\\\\\\\mathbf{F} = q\\\\\\\\,\\\\\\\\mathbf{v} \\\\\\\\times \\\\\\\\mathbf{B}\\\\\\\\).\\\\n\\\\nFrom this follow key motions (as shown in standard plasma-physics treatments and educational material):[2][3][6]\\\\n\\\\n- A component of velocity **perpendicular** to \\\\\\\\(\\\\\\\\mathbf{B}\\\\\\\\) causes **circular gyro-motion** around the field line at the Larmor radius.  \\\\n- A component **parallel** to \\\\\\\\(\\\\\\\\mathbf{B}\\\\\\\\) feels no magnetic force and moves freely along the field.[2]  \\\\n\\\\nCombined, ions and electrons **spiral** along magnetic field lines: they are tightly bound across the field but free to move along it.[2][3][6]\\\\n\\\\nThis leads to the confinement idea:\\\\n\\\\n- Shape the magnetic field so that **field lines are closed** (e.g., in a torus), forming a “magnetic bottle.”  \\\\n- Particles spiral around these closed lines, remaining away from material walls.[1][3][6]\\\\n\\\\nThe stronger the magnetic field:\\\\n\\\\n- The **smaller** the Larmor radius.  \\\\n- The **slower** cross-field drifts and diffusion.  \\\\n- The **better** the confinement.[2][3]\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### 3. From single particles to plasma: collective and MHD behavior\\\\n\\\\nAt fusion-relevant densities, the plasma’s own currents and charges significantly modify the externally applied magnetic field, and the medium must be treated collectively.[2][3][7] This is described by **magnetohydrodynamics (MHD)**:\\\\n\\\\n- The plasma behaves like a conducting fluid embedded in magnetic field lines.  \\\\n- Magnetic field lines are often described as “frozen in” to the plasma: fluid elements move along field lines, and dragging the plasma across the field tends to drag the lines with it.[2]\\\\n\\\\nKey implications for magnetic confinement:\\\\n\\\\n- **Pressure balance:** Plasma pressure pushes outward, magnetic pressure and tension pull inward. Stable confinement demands that the magnetic field be strong enough and appropriately shaped to counter plasma pressure and currents.[3][7]  \\\\n- **Instabilities:** Certain pressure/current configurations are unstable (e.g., kink, ballooning, interchange instabilities), leading to bulging, twisting, or breaking of confined regions and degraded confinement.[2][3][6][7]  \\\\n- **Turbulence:** Small-scale fluctuations and turbulence cause enhanced transport of heat and particles across field lines, reducing the effective confinement time below what classical single-particle theory would predict.[2][3][7]\\\\n\\\\nDesigning a successful magnetic confinement system is largely about **finding magnetic geometries and operating regimes that avoid or tame these instabilities** and minimize turbulent transport.[3][6][7]\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### 4. Magnetic geometry in practice: toroidal devices\\\\n\\\\nBecause particles stream freely along field lines, the field lines themselves must not intersect walls, which leads naturally to **toroidal (doughnut-shaped)** configurations:[1][5][6]\\\\n\\\\n- **Tokamak:**  \\\\n  - Strong toroidal field from external coils.  \\\\n  - Large plasma current generates a poloidal field, twisting field lines into helical paths, improving confinement and stability.[5][6][7]  \\\\n- **Stellarator:**  \\\\n  - Uses 3D-shaped external coils to create the required helical fields; does not rely on a large plasma current, which avoids some current-driven instabilities but demands complex coil engineering.[5][6][7]\\\\n\\\\nTwist in the field lines helps cancel or average out systematic drifts that would otherwise move particles to the wall.[2][6]\\\\n\\\\nOther configurations (mirror machines, reversed-field pinches, spherical tokamaks, etc.) explore different ways of shaping \\\\\\\\(\\\\\\\\mathbf{B}\\\\\\\\), but modern mainstream MCF focuses on tokamaks and stellarators.[5][6][7]\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### 5. Energy balance and the Lawson criterion\\\\n\\\\nTo generate net power, the fusion plasma must satisfy an **energy balance condition**: fusion power produced must equal or exceed total power lost (radiation, conduction, convection, particle escape).[6][7]\\\\n\\\\nFor a D–T plasma, this condition is commonly expressed as the **Lawson criterion**, which relates:\\\\n\\\\n- **n** – plasma particle density  \\\\n- **T** – temperature  \\\\n- **τ\\\\\\\\_E** – energy confinement time (a measure of how long energy stays in the plasma before being lost)\\\\n\\\\nIn one common form, the Lawson criterion requires that the **triple product** \\\\\\\\(n T \\\\\\\\tau_E\\\\\\\\) exceed a critical value for ignition (self-sustaining fusion without external heating) or for net energy gain.[6][7]\\\\n\\\\nConceptually:\\\\n\\\\n- Fusion power density \\\\\\\\(\\\\\\\\propto n^2 \\\\\\\\langle \\\\\\\\sigma v \\\\\\\\rangle\\\\\\\\), where \\\\\\\\(\\\\\\\\langle \\\\\\\\sigma v \\\\\\\\rangle\\\\\\\\) increases with temperature up to an optimum.  \\\\n- Loss power density \\\\\\\\(\\\\\\\\propto \\\\\\\\frac{3 n T}{\\\\\\\\tau_E}\\\\\\\\) (roughly, energy per particle divided by confinement time).  \\\\n- Setting fusion power ≥ loss power gives a condition on \\\\\\\\(n T \\\\\\\\tau_E\\\\\\\\).[6][7]\\\\n\\\\nFor D–T at ∼10–20 keV, the required triple product is on the order of \\\\\\\\(10^{21}\\\\\\\\,\\\\\\\\text{keV·s·m}^{-3}\\\\\\\\) (order-of-magnitude; exact numbers depend on detailed assumptions), and modern large tokamaks operate near or approaching this regime in brief pulses.[6][7]\\\\n\\\\n**Role of the Lawson criterion in MCF:**\\\\n\\\\n- It defines the **minimum combination** of density, temperature, and confinement time needed for practical fusion.  \\\\n- Because the temperature window is fairly constrained by fusion cross sections, MCF devices mostly trade off **density versus confinement time**:  \\\\n  - Magnetic confinement operates at relatively **low density** and **long τ\\\\\\\\_E** (milliseconds to seconds or longer).  \\\\n  - Inertial confinement operates at very **high density** and extremely **short τ\\\\\\\\_E** (nanoseconds).  \\\\n- It provides a quantitative **performance metric**: experiments report their achieved \\\\\\\\(n T \\\\\\\\tau_E\\\\\\\\) and compare to the Lawson threshold for ignition or for specific gain factors.[6][7]\\\\n\\\\nIn short, the Lawson criterion translates “good enough confinement” into a precise inequality involving measurable plasma parameters.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### 6. Why magnetic confinement is hard\\\\n\\\\nLinking the physics pieces:\\\\n\\\\n- **Single-particle physics** explains why strong magnetic fields can, in principle, confine hot plasmas away from walls.  \\\\n- **Collective and MHD physics** explain why real plasmas develop currents, instabilities, and turbulence that degrade that ideal confinement.  \\\\n- The **Lawson criterion** states the quantitative target: despite all losses, achieve a triple product high enough that fusion heating balances or exceeds losses.\\\\n\\\\nMajor technical and physics challenges in MCF include:[3][4][6][7]\\\\n\\\\n- Achieving and sustaining **multi-tesla magnetic fields** with high precision.  \\\\n- Controlling **MHD instabilities** and turbulent transport to attain long τ\\\\\\\\_E.  \\\\n- Handling **extreme heat and particle loads** where confined plasma meets material surfaces (divertors, first wall).[3]  \\\\n- Integrating materials, superconducting magnets, heating systems, and control systems to operate reliably for long durations.[3][6][7]\\\\n\\\\nAll of these are pursued with the Lawson criterion in mind: improving confinement time and allowable density at a given temperature to reach or surpass the ignition and net-gain conditions.\\\\n\\\\nIf you’d like, I can next walk through the Lawson criterion derivation step-by-step from the energy {`})]}),`\n`,_jsx(_components.span,{className:`line`,children:_jsx(_components.span,{children:`        \"content\": \"Magnetic confinement fusion uses strong magnetic fields to trap a very hot, ionized gas (plasma) so that light nuclei collide and fuse faster than the energy is lost, and the Lawson criterion quantifies the minimum combination of plasma density, temperature, and confinement time required for this to produce net energy. The core physics is charged-particle motion in magnetic fields (guiding centers following field lines plus gyration and drifts), collective plasma stability, and energy balance; the Lawson criterion is the formal expression of that energy balance.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### 1. Why fusion needs confinement\\\\n\\\\nFor deuterium–tritium (D–T) fusion to occur at an appreciable rate, the plasma must reach temperatures of order \\\\\\\\(10^8\\\\\\\\) K (∼10 keV), hotter than the Sun’s core, so that nuclei can overcome the Coulomb repulsion and get close enough for the strong nuclear force to fuse them.[1][4][6] At these temperatures:\\\\n\\\\n- All atoms are ionized → a **plasma** of electrons and ions.[1][4][6]  \\\\n- No solid material can touch the plasma; it would vaporize instantly.[1][4]\\\\n\\\\nSo fusion requires:\\\\n\\\\n- **Heating** the fuel to fusion temperatures.  \\\\n- **Confining** it long enough and dense enough that many fusion reactions occur before the energy escapes.[4][6]\\\\n\\\\nIn stars, gravity provides confinement; in labs, strong magnetic fields are used instead.[4][6]\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### 2. Single-particle motion: how magnetic fields confine charges\\\\n\\\\nThe basic building block is the Lorentz force on a charged particle in a magnetic field: \\\\\\\\(\\\\\\\\mathbf{F} = q\\\\\\\\,\\\\\\\\mathbf{v} \\\\\\\\times \\\\\\\\mathbf{B}\\\\\\\\).\\\\n\\\\nFrom this follow key motions (as shown in standard plasma-physics treatments and educational material):[2][3][6]\\\\n\\\\n- A component of velocity **perpendicular** to \\\\\\\\(\\\\\\\\mathbf{B}\\\\\\\\) causes **circular gyro-motion** around the field line at the Larmor radius.  \\\\n- A component **parallel** to \\\\\\\\(\\\\\\\\mathbf{B}\\\\\\\\) feels no magnetic force and moves freely along the field.[2]  \\\\n\\\\nCombined, ions and electrons **spiral** along magnetic field lines: they are tightly bound across the field but free to move along it.[2][3][6]\\\\n\\\\nThis leads to the confinement idea:\\\\n\\\\n- Shape the magnetic field so that **field lines are closed** (e.g., in a torus), forming a “magnetic bottle.”  \\\\n- Particles spiral around these closed lines, remaining away from material walls.[1][3][6]\\\\n\\\\nThe stronger the magnetic field:\\\\n\\\\n- The **smaller** the Larmor radius.  \\\\n- The **slower** cross-field drifts and diffusion.  \\\\n- The **better** the confinement.[2][3]\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### 3. From single particles to plasma: collective and MHD behavior\\\\n\\\\nAt fusion-relevant densities, the plasma’s own currents and charges significantly modify the externally applied magnetic field, and the medium must be treated collectively.[2][3][7] This is described by **magnetohydrodynamics (MHD)**:\\\\n\\\\n- The plasma behaves like a conducting fluid embedded in magnetic field lines.  \\\\n- Magnetic field lines are often described as “frozen in” to the plasma: fluid elements move along field lines, and dragging the plasma across the field tends to drag the lines with it.[2]\\\\n\\\\nKey implications for magnetic confinement:\\\\n\\\\n- **Pressure balance:** Plasma pressure pushes outward, magnetic pressure and tension pull inward. Stable confinement demands that the magnetic field be strong enough and appropriately shaped to counter plasma pressure and currents.[3][7]  \\\\n- **Instabilities:** Certain pressure/current configurations are unstable (e.g., kink, ballooning, interchange instabilities), leading to bulging, twisting, or breaking of confined regions and degraded confinement.[2][3][6][7]  \\\\n- **Turbulence:** Small-scale fluctuations and turbulence cause enhanced transport of heat and particles across field lines, reducing the effective confinement time below what classical single-particle theory would predict.[2][3][7]\\\\n\\\\nDesigning a successful magnetic confinement system is largely about **finding magnetic geometries and operating regimes that avoid or tame these instabilities** and minimize turbulent transport.[3][6][7]\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### 4. Magnetic geometry in practice: toroidal devices\\\\n\\\\nBecause particles stream freely along field lines, the field lines themselves must not intersect walls, which leads naturally to **toroidal (doughnut-shaped)** configurations:[1][5][6]\\\\n\\\\n- **Tokamak:**  \\\\n  - Strong toroidal field from external coils.  \\\\n  - Large plasma current generates a poloidal field, twisting field lines into helical paths, improving confinement and stability.[5][6][7]  \\\\n- **Stellarator:**  \\\\n  - Uses 3D-shaped external coils to create the required helical fields; does not rely on a large plasma current, which avoids some current-driven instabilities but demands complex coil engineering.[5][6][7]\\\\n\\\\nTwist in the field lines helps cancel or average out systematic drifts that would otherwise move particles to the wall.[2][6]\\\\n\\\\nOther configurations (mirror machines, reversed-field pinches, spherical tokamaks, etc.) explore different ways of shaping \\\\\\\\(\\\\\\\\mathbf{B}\\\\\\\\), but modern mainstream MCF focuses on tokamaks and stellarators.[5][6][7]\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### 5. Energy balance and the Lawson criterion\\\\n\\\\nTo generate net power, the fusion plasma must satisfy an **energy balance condition**: fusion power produced must equal or exceed total power lost (radiation, conduction, convection, particle escape).[6][7]\\\\n\\\\nFor a D–T plasma, this condition is commonly expressed as the **Lawson criterion**, which relates:\\\\n\\\\n- **n** – plasma particle density  \\\\n- **T** – temperature  \\\\n- **τ\\\\\\\\_E** – energy confinement time (a measure of how long energy stays in the plasma before being lost)\\\\n\\\\nIn one common form, the Lawson criterion requires that the **triple product** \\\\\\\\(n T \\\\\\\\tau_E\\\\\\\\) exceed a critical value for ignition (self-sustaining fusion without external heating) or for net energy gain.[6][7]\\\\n\\\\nConceptually:\\\\n\\\\n- Fusion power density \\\\\\\\(\\\\\\\\propto n^2 \\\\\\\\langle \\\\\\\\sigma v \\\\\\\\rangle\\\\\\\\), where \\\\\\\\(\\\\\\\\langle \\\\\\\\sigma v \\\\\\\\rangle\\\\\\\\) increases with temperature up to an optimum.  \\\\n- Loss power density \\\\\\\\(\\\\\\\\propto \\\\\\\\frac{3 n T}{\\\\\\\\tau_E}\\\\\\\\) (roughly, energy per particle divided by confinement time).  \\\\n- Setting fusion power ≥ loss power gives a condition on \\\\\\\\(n T \\\\\\\\tau_E\\\\\\\\).[6][7]\\\\n\\\\nFor D–T at ∼10–20 keV, the required triple product is on the order of \\\\\\\\(10^{21}\\\\\\\\,\\\\\\\\text{keV·s·m}^{-3}\\\\\\\\) (order-of-magnitude; exact numbers depend on detailed assumptions), and modern large tokamaks operate near or approaching this regime in brief pulses.[6][7]\\\\n\\\\n**Role of the Lawson criterion in MCF:**\\\\n\\\\n- It defines the **minimum combination** of density, temperature, and confinement time needed for practical fusion.  \\\\n- Because the temperature window is fairly constrained by fusion cross sections, MCF devices mostly trade off **density versus confinement time**:  \\\\n  - Magnetic confinement operates at relatively **low density** and **long τ\\\\\\\\_E** (milliseconds to seconds or longer).  \\\\n  - Inertial confinement operates at very **high density** and extremely **short τ\\\\\\\\_E** (nanoseconds).  \\\\n- It provides a quantitative **performance metric**: experiments report their achieved \\\\\\\\(n T \\\\\\\\tau_E\\\\\\\\) and compare to the Lawson threshold for ignition or for specific gain factors.[6][7]\\\\n\\\\nIn short, the Lawson criterion translates “good enough confinement” into a precise inequality involving measurable plasma parameters.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n### 6. Why magnetic confinement is hard\\\\n\\\\nLinking the physics pieces:\\\\n\\\\n- **Single-particle physics** explains why strong magnetic fields can, in principle, confine hot plasmas away from walls.  \\\\n- **Collective and MHD physics** explain why real plasmas develop currents, instabilities, and turbulence that degrade that ideal confinement.  \\\\n- The **Lawson criterion** states the quantitative target: despite all losses, achieve a triple product high enough that fusion heating balances or exceeds losses.\\\\n\\\\nMajor technical and physics challenges in MCF include:[3][4][6][7]\\\\n\\\\n- Achieving and sustaining **multi-tesla magnetic fields** with high precision.  \\\\n- Controlling **MHD instabilities** and turbulent transport to attain long τ\\\\\\\\_E.  \\\\n- Handling **extreme heat and particle loads** where confined plasma meets material surfaces (divertors, first wall).[3]  \\\\n- Integrating materials, superconducting magnets, heating systems, and control systems to operate reliably for long durations.[3][6][7]\\\\n\\\\nAll of these are pursued with the Lawson criterion in mind: improving confinement time and allowable density at a given temperature to reach or surpass the ignition and net-gain conditions.\\\\n\\\\nIf you’d like, I can next walk through the Lawson criterion derivation step-by-step from the energy
